newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: KERNOT SAYS SALE OF TELSTRA A LONG WAY OFF
Australian Democrats leader Cheryl Kernot says the sale of Telstra is a long way from being resolved.
Senator Kernot also says the decisions of independent senators, Mal Colston and Brian Harradine, on Telstra, won't be known till the last minute.
She says she doesn't think Senator Colston has done a deal with the Government on Telstra to get the deputy presidency of the Senate.
Senator Kernot says Senator Colston has had, and still has, concerns about regional Telstra workers in Queensland.
COLSTON: MANDATE ON TELSTRA SALE A GREY AREA
Queensland Independent Senator, Mal Colston, says the Federal Government has no clear-cut mandate for the partial sale of Telstra.
But Senator Colston says the sale is tied up with a number of other issues.
His comments follow concerns raised by Brian Harradine, who's also an independent Senator, about the Government's longer term plans for the telecommunications carrier.
Senator Harradine says he's concerned about Communications Minister Richard Alston's view that the privatisation in full of Telstra is both inevitable and desirable.
But Senator Colston says the Prime Minister's dismissal of Senator Alston's comments has negated them.
The government needs the support of both Senators to get its Telstra bill through the Senate.
SENATOR SUPPORTS URANIUM MINING
The chairman of the Senate Committee examining uranium mining says further uranium mining would reap huge export benefits for Australia.
Liberal Senator Grant Chapman is taking evidence today from traditional owners in Kakadu National Park in the Northern Territory on a further mine in the area.
Senator Chapman says another uranium mine in Kakadu would benefit the local area, the Northern Territory and Australia.
But he's conceded there're people who have doubts and says the committee will take their views into account to produce a report that's balanced.
DOCTORS ACCUSED OF COLLUSION
A contract dispute between medical specialists and Mildura Base Hospital, in north west Victoria, is being investigated by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).
The ACCCC says it's received a complaint alleging collusion by specialists during the dispute.
The complaint centres on the doctors' refusal, through a negotiator they'd appointed, to negotiate contracts individually.
The ACCC has written to all parties requesting information. ----
QLD ALP SECRETARY UNDER FIRE
An inquiry's been told there's evidence which could support a case of bribery against Labor's Queensland secretary, Mike Kaiser.
The inquiry into the deal between the ALP and the Sporting Shooters' Association before last year's state election is taking final legal submissions .
Counsel assisting, Cedric Hampson QC, has also suggested there's evidence to bring bribery charges against Sporting Shooters' President Bob Green and the association's Treasurer Terry Rafter.
Mr Hampson hasn't made a direct recommendation about former Premier Wayne Goss but says his involvement in the matter did influence the electoral conduct of the Sporting Shooters' Association.
CANBERRA TO SYDNEY TRAIN NOT LIKELY BEFORE 2000
Federal Transport Minister John Sharp says delays by the New South Wales Government have effectively ruled out having the proposed Sydney to Canberra high-speed train running for the 2000 Olympics.
The two billion dollar project has the backing of the Federal and A.C.T. Governments but it is still awaiting approval by New South Wales.
The project is linked to the proposed upgrade of Canberra airport to international standard.
HEALTH MINISTER MAY HAVE KNOWN PREMIUMS WOULD RISE
Opposition Health spokesman, Michael Lee, says the Health Minister has some explaining to do if he knew before the budget there would be increases in health insurance premiums.
A newspaper report states Health Minister Michael Wooldridge's office was informed of a proposed premium rise by one company some weeks before the budget was announced.
A spokeswoman for the Minister won't confirm details but says Dr Wooldridge was advised in an "ad hoc" way.
Prime Minister John Howard earlier said neither the government nor the Health Minister knew of the increases before the budget.
